paragraphs.heading: A body of nations
paragraphs.text: The United Nations (UN) is an organization of governments founded when its Charter was signed on 26 June 1945. Its stated aims are to keep international peace and security, build friendly relations between countries, encourage cooperation, and serve as a place where countries coordinate their actions toward these goals. With 193 member states, nearly every sovereign state in the world, it is the largest international organization. Its headquarters is in New York City, with other major offices in Geneva, Nairobi, Vienna and The Hague. The Holy See and the State of Palestine sit alongside them as observer states.

paragraphs.heading: How it is built and what it does
paragraphs.text: The UN has six main parts: the General Assembly, the Security Council, the Economic and Social Council, the International Court of Justice, the Secretariat and the Trusteeship Council. Together with specialised and related agencies, they form what is called the UN System. Its main focus has been economic and social development, especially during the wave of decolonization in the middle of the 20th century. It currently runs 11 peacekeeping missions, from the Middle East and Kashmir to South Sudan and the Central African Republic. Many of its officials and agencies have won the Nobel Peace Prize, yet it has also been criticised as ineffective, biased and corrupt.

paragraphs.heading: The League of Nations
paragraphs.text: The UN replaced an earlier body. During World War I, leaders including US President Woodrow Wilson called for a world body to keep the peace. After the war the winning Allies settled peace terms at the Paris Peace Conference, and the League of Nations came into being on 10 January 1920, once its Covenant, ratified by 42 nations, took effect. The United States never joined. Almost all of the League's major decisions needed every member to agree, a rule meant to protect each nation's sovereignty.

paragraphs.heading: Why the League failed
paragraphs.text: The League often failed to act. Forty nations voted that Japan should leave Manchuria, which it occupied; Japan voted against and quit the League instead. It also failed over Italy's war on Ethiopia, even after Emperor Haile Selassie I appealed for help at Geneva in 1936 and calls for sanctions came to nothing. When World War II began in 1939 the League effectively shut down, and one of its last acts was to expel the Soviet Union for invading Finland.

paragraphs.heading: A name born in wartime
paragraphs.text: The first step toward the UN was the Declaration of St. James's Palace, which came out of a conference of the Allies in London on 12 June 1941. By August 1941 Roosevelt and Churchill had drafted the Atlantic Charter, setting goals for the world after the war. Roosevelt, seen as a founder of the UN, coined the name "United Nations" for the Allied countries, and Churchill accepted it. During the war it became the Allies' official name, and to join, countries had to sign the Declaration by the United Nations and declare war on the Axis powers.

paragraphs.heading: Designing the new body
paragraphs.text: In October 1943 the Moscow Conference produced a declaration signed by the Allied Big Four (China, Britain, the Soviet Union and the United States) calling for a general international organization "at the earliest possible date". It was the first public sign that a new body would replace the League of Nations. Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin discussed the idea soon after at Tehran. At Dumbarton Oaks, from 21 September to 7 October 1944, the Big Four delegations agreed on the new body's aims, structure and workings, and the last issues were settled only after the Yalta conference in February 1945 and further talks with the Soviets.
